title: Don't be THAT GUY in 2024
summary: Using five archetypes from his commercial gym, NH lists the time-wasting habits to avoid: never progressing load, turning supersets into sloppy circuits, half-rep ego lifting, ignoring form, and never training close to failure (plus phone use mid-set). He admits his own sin is creeping range of motion with too much weight.
claims: Lifting the same weight for six months is a plateau; even a novice who does this wastes newbie gains
'Muscles can't see weight' is only partly true: muscles feel the load, and without added stress they have no reason to grow
Every natural with a good physique lifts heavy, not as heavy as strength athletes but far heavier than the empty bar
Whether training for sport, function or bodybuilding, progression must happen or you are lifting for nothing
There is no time limit between superset exercises; take a minute to walk between stations if needed, you still save time
Never let a superset dictate load or technique; rushed supersets with baby weights become circuit training and garbage volume
Cardinal superset sin: supersetting the same muscle three or four exercises in a row; performance suffers if you train with intensity
Control the negative; the weight should not lead you
Skinny under-recovered under-eaters tend to grow best from low volume, high intensity and long recovery; what they do outside the gym matters most
To grow a muscle you must go through range of motion; quarter squats with huge loads grow nothing
Overloaded half squats are dangerous 'squat roulette': going slightly too deep loses control, and these lifters don't know how to bail
Insisting on proper form is necessary because beginners need clear good-vs-bad rules; once you have the foundation you can get exotic, e.g. rounding the upper back
Strong lifters like a 900 lb rounded-back deadlifter or Arnold's body English do not justify sloppy form for novices; earn it first
Most gym-goers never train close to failure; stopping a set when all reps look identical is just warming up
A rep range should be chosen around the weight so that you are near failure at the target rep, not stopped arbitrarily at 10
RPE and RIR only make sense once you have trained to failure many times; beginners need to learn failure first
90% of people consuming fitness content are complete beginners who need the basics repeated, not advanced nuance
Don't train for a fixed duration; pick the work and let it take what it takes. 45-60 minutes of hard sets will exhaust most people
Browsing your phone between sets is fine, but using it during a set kills focus and growth
His own recurring sin: stacking too much weight and shortening range of motion until he resets with less load and proper reps
